1 import { CodeExampleStack } from "@/components/code-example"; 2 3 export const title = "Adding custom styles"; 4 export const description = "Best practices for adding your own custom styles in Tailwind projects."; 5 6 Often the biggest challenge when working with a framework is figuring out what you’re supposed to do when there’s something you need that the framework doesn’t handle for you. 7 8 Tailwind has been designed from the ground up to be extensible and customizable, so that no matter what you’re building you never feel like you’re fighting the framework. 9 10 This guide covers topics like customizing your design tokens, how to break out of those constraints when necessary, adding your own custom CSS, and extending the framework with plugins. 11 12 ## Customizing your theme 13 14 If you want to change things like your color palette, spacing scale, typography scale, or breakpoints, add your customizations using the `@theme` directive in your CSS: 15 16 ```css 17 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 18 @theme { 19 --font-display: "Satoshi", "sans-serif"; 20 21 --breakpoint-3xl: 120rem; 22 23 --color-avocado-100: oklch(0.99 0 0); 24 --color-avocado-200: oklch(0.98 0.04 113.22); 25 --color-avocado-300: oklch(0.94 0.11 115.03); 26 --color-avocado-400: oklch(0.92 0.19 114.08); 27 --color-avocado-500: oklch(0.84 0.18 117.33); 28 --color-avocado-600: oklch(0.53 0.12 118.34); 29 30 --ease-fluid: cubic-bezier(0.3, 0, 0, 1); 31 --ease-snappy: cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1); 32 33 /* ... */ 34 } 35 ``` 36 37 Learn more about customizing your theme in the [theme variables documentation](/docs/theme). 38 39 ## Using arbitrary values 40 41 While you can usually build the bulk of a well-crafted design using a constrained set of design tokens, once in a while you need to break out of those constraints to get things pixel-perfect. 42 43 When you find yourself really needing something like `top: 117px` to get a background image in just the right spot, use Tailwind's square bracket notation to generate a class on the fly with any arbitrary value: 44 45 ```html 46 47 48
49 50
51 ``` 52 53 This is basically like inline styles, with the major benefit that you can combine it with interactive modifiers like `hover` and responsive modifiers like `lg`: 54 55 ```html 56 57 58
59 60
61 ``` 62 63 This works for everything in the framework, including things like background colors, font sizes, pseudo-element content, and more: 64 65 ```html 66 67 68
69 70
71 ``` 72 73 If you're referencing a CSS variable as an arbitrary value, you can use the custom property syntax: 74 75 ```html 76 77 78
79 80
81 ``` 82 83 This is just a shorthand for fill-{'[var(--my-brand-color)]'} that adds the `var()` function for you automatically. 84 85 ### Arbitrary properties 86 87 If you ever need to use a CSS property that Tailwind doesn't include a utility for out of the box, you can also use square bracket notation to write completely arbitrary CSS: 88 89 ```html 90 91 92
93 94
95 ``` 96 97 This is _really_ like inline styles, but again with the benefit that you can use modifiers: 98 99 ```html 100 101 102
103 104
105 ``` 106 107 This can be useful for things like CSS variables as well, especially when they need to change under different conditions: 108 109 ```html 110 111 112
113 114
115 ``` 116 117 ### Arbitrary variants 118 119 Arbitrary _variants_ are like arbitrary values but for doing on-the-fly selector modification, like you can with built-in pseudo-class variants like `hover:{utility}` or responsive variants like `md:{utility}` but using square bracket notation directly in your HTML. 120 121 ```html 122 123 124
    125 {#each items as item} 126
  • {item}
    • 127 {/each} 128
129 ``` 130 131 Learn more in the [arbitrary variants](/docs/hover-focus-and-other-states#using-arbitrary-variants) documentation. 132 133 ### Handling whitespace 134 135 When an arbitrary value needs to contain a space, use an underscore (`_`) instead and Tailwind will automatically convert it to a space at build-time: 136 137 ```html 138 139 140
141 142
143 ``` 144 145 In situations where underscores are common but spaces are invalid, Tailwind will preserve the underscore instead of converting it to a space, for example in URLs: 146 147 ```html 148 149 150
151 152
153 ``` 154 155 In the rare case that you actually need to use an underscore but it's ambiguous because a space is valid as well, escape the underscore with a backslash and Tailwind won't convert it to a space: 156 157 ```html 158 159 160
161 162
163 ``` 164 165 If you're using something like JSX where the backslash is stripped from the rendered HTML, use [String.raw()](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Global_Objects/String/raw) so the backslash isn't treated as a JavaScript escape character: 166 167 ```jsx 168
169 170
171 ``` 172 173 ### Resolving ambiguities 174 175 Many utilities in Tailwind share a common namespace but map to different CSS properties. For example `text-lg` and `text-black` both share the `text-` namespace, but one is for `font-size` and the other is for `color`. 176 177 When using arbitrary values, Tailwind can generally handle this ambiguity automatically based on the value you pass in: 178 179 ```html 180 181 182 183
...
184 185 186
...
187 ``` 188 189 Sometimes it really is ambiguous though, for example when using CSS variables: 190 191 ```html 192 193 194
...
195 ``` 196 197 In these situations, you can "hint" the underlying type to Tailwind by adding a [CSS data type](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_Types) before the value: 198 199 ```html 200 201 202 203
...
204 205 206
...
207 ``` 208 209 ## Using custom CSS 210 211 While Tailwind is designed to handle the bulk of your styling needs, there is nothing stopping you from just writing plain CSS when you need to: 212 213 ```css 214 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 215 @import "tailwindcss"; 216 217 /* [!code highlight:4] */ 218 .my-custom-style { 219 /* ... */ 220 } 221 ``` 222 223 ### Adding base styles 224 225 If you just want to set some defaults for the page (like the text color, background color, or font family), the easiest option is just adding some classes to the `html` or `body` elements: 226 227 ```html 228 229 230 231 232 233 234 ``` 235 236 This keeps your base styling decisions in your markup alongside all of your other styles, instead of hiding them in a separate file. 237 238 If you want to add your own default base styles for specific HTML elements, use the `@layer` directive to add those styles to Tailwind's `base` layer: 239 240 ```css 241 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 242 /* [!code highlight:2] */ 243 @layer base { 244 h1 { 245 font-size: var(--text-2xl); 246 } 247 248 h2 { 249 font-size: var(--text-xl); 250 } 251 /* [!code highlight:2] */ 252 } 253 ``` 254 255 ### Adding component classes 256 257 Use the `components` layer for any more complicated classes you want to add to your project that you'd still like to be able to override with utility classes. 258 259 Traditionally these would be classes like `card`, `btn`, `badge` — that kind of thing. 260 261 ```css 262 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 263 /* [!code highlight:2] */ 264 @layer components { 265 .card { 266 background-color: var(--color-white); 267 border-radius: var(--radius-lg); 268 padding: --spacing(6); 269 box-shadow: var(--shadow-xl); 270 } 271 /* [!code highlight:2] */ 272 } 273 ``` 274 275 By defining component classes in the `components` layer, you can still use utility classes to override them when necessary: 276 277 ```html 278 279 280 281
282 283
284 ``` 285 286 Using Tailwind you probably don't need these types of classes as often as you think. Read our guide on [managing duplication](/docs/styling-with-utility-classes#managing-duplication) for our recommendations. 287 288 The `components` layer is also a good place to put custom styles for any third-party components you're using: 289 290 ```css 291 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 292 @layer components { 293 .select2-dropdown { 294 /* ... */ 295 } 296 } 297 ``` 298 299 ### Using variants 300 301 Use the `@variant` directive to apply a Tailwind variant within custom CSS: 302 303 304 305 ```css 306 /* [!code filename:app.css] */ 307 .my-element { 308 background: white; 309 310 /* [!code highlight:4] */ 311 @variant dark { 312 background: black; 313 } 314 } 315 ``` 316 317 ```css 318 /* [!code filename:Compiled CSS] */ 319 .my-element { 320 background: white; 321 322 /* [!code highlight:4] */ 323 @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { 324 background: black; 325 } 326 } 327 ``` 328 329 330 331 If you need to apply multiple variants at the same time, stack them using the same syntax you would in HTML: 332 333 334 335 ```css 336 /* [!code filename:app.css] */ 337 .my-element { 338 background: white; 339 340 /* [!code highlight:4] */ 341 @variant hover:focus { 342 background: black; 343 } 344 } 345 ``` 346 347 ```css 348 /* [!code filename:Compiled CSS] */ 349 .my-element { 350 background: white; 351 352 /* [!code highlight:8] */ 353 &:hover { 354 @media (hover: hover) { 355 &:focus { 356 background: black; 357 } 358 } 359 } 360 } 361 ``` 362 363 364 365 To apply the same styles for multiple variants, separate each variant with a comma: 366 367 368 369 ```css 370 /* [!code filename:app.css] */ 371 .my-element { 372 background: white; 373 374 /* [!code highlight:4] */ 375 @variant hover, focus { 376 background: black; 377 } 378 } 379 ``` 380 381 ```css 382 /* [!code filename:Compiled CSS] */ 383 .my-element { 384 background: white; 385 386 /* [!code highlight:6] */ 387 &:hover { 388 @media (hover: hover) { 389 background: black; 390 } 391 } 392 393 /* [!code highlight:4] */ 394 &:focus { 395 background: black; 396 } 397 } 398 ``` 399 400 401 402 ## Adding custom utilities 403 404 ### Simple utilities 405 406 In addition to using the utilities that ship with Tailwind, you can also add your own custom utilities. This can be useful when there's a CSS feature you'd like to use in your project that Tailwind doesn't include utilities for out of the box. 407 408 Use the `@utility` directive to add a custom utility to your project: 409 410 ```css 411 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 412 @utility content-auto { 413 content-visibility: auto; 414 } 415 ``` 416 417 You can now use this utility in your HTML: 418 419 ```html 420 421 422
423 424
425 ``` 426 427 It will also work with variants like `hover`, `focus` and `lg`: 428 429 ```html 430 431 432
433 434
435 ``` 436 437 Custom utilities are automatically inserted into the `utilities` layer along with all of the built-in utilities in the framework. 438 439 ### Complex utilities 440 441 If your custom utility is more complex than a single class name, use nesting to define the utility: 442 443 ```css 444 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 445 @utility scrollbar-hidden { 446 &::-webkit-scrollbar { 447 display: none; 448 } 449 } 450 ``` 451 452 ### Functional utilities 453 454 In addition to registering simple utilities with the `@utility` directive, you can also register functional utilities that accept an argument: 455 456 ```css 457 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 458 @utility tab-* { 459 /* prettier-ignore */ 460 tab-size: --value(--tab-size-*); 461 } 462 ``` 463 464 The special `--value()` function is used to resolve the utility value. 465 466 #### Matching theme values 467 468 Use the `--value(--theme-key-*)` syntax to resolve the utility value against a set of theme keys: 469 470 ```css 471 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 472 @theme { 473 --tab-size-2: 2; 474 --tab-size-4: 4; 475 --tab-size-github: 8; 476 } 477 478 @utility tab-* { 479 /* [!code highlight:2] */ 480 /* prettier-ignore */ 481 tab-size: --value(--tab-size-*); 482 } 483 ``` 484 485 This will match utilities like `tab-2`, `tab-4`, and `tab-github`. 486 487 #### Bare values 488 489 To resolve the value as a bare value, use the `--value({type})` syntax, where `{type}` is the data type you want to validate the bare value as: 490 491 ```css 492 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 493 @utility tab-* { 494 tab-size: --value(integer); 495 } 496 ``` 497 498 This will match utilities like `tab-1` and `tab-76`. 499 500 Available bare value data types are: `number`, `integer`, `ratio`, and `percentage`. 501 502 #### Literal values 503 504 To support literal values, use the `--value('literal')` syntax (notice the quotes): 505 506 ```css 507 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 508 @utility tab-* { 509 tab-size: --value("inherit", "initial", "unset"); 510 } 511 ``` 512 513 This will match utilities like `tab-inherit`, `tab-initial`, and `tab-unset`. 514 515 #### Arbitrary values 516 517 To support arbitrary values, use the `--value([{type}])` syntax (notice the square brackets) to tell Tailwind which types are supported as an arbitrary value: 518 519 ```css 520 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 521 @utility tab-* { 522 tab-size: --value([integer]); 523 } 524 ``` 525 526 This will match utilities like `tab-[1]` and `tab-[76]`. 527 528 Available arbitrary value data types are: `absolute-size`, `angle`, `bg-size`, `color`, `family-name`, `generic-name`, `image`, `integer`, `length`, `line-width`, `number`, `percentage`, `position`, `ratio`, `relative-size`, `url`, `vector`, and `*`. 529 530 #### Supporting theme, bare, and arbitrary values together 531 532 All three forms of the `--value()` function can be used within a rule as multiple declarations, and any declarations that fail to resolve will be omitted in the output: 533 534 ```css 535 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 536 @theme { 537 --tab-size-github: 8; 538 } 539 540 @utility tab-* { 541 tab-size: --value([integer]); 542 tab-size: --value(integer); 543 /* prettier-ignore */ 544 tab-size: --value(--tab-size-*); 545 } 546 ``` 547 548 This makes it possible to treat the value differently in each case if necessary, for example translating a bare integer to a percentage: 549 550 ```css 551 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 552 @utility opacity-* { 553 opacity: --value([percentage]); 554 /* [!code highlight:2] */ 555 opacity: calc(--value(integer) * 1%); 556 /* prettier-ignore */ 557 opacity: --value(--opacity-*); 558 } 559 ``` 560 561 The `--value()` function can also take multiple arguments and resolve them left to right if you don't need to treat the return value differently in different cases: 562 563 ```css 564 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 565 @theme { 566 --tab-size-github: 8; 567 } 568 569 @utility tab-* { 570 /* [!code highlight:2] */ 571 /* prettier-ignore */ 572 tab-size: --value(--tab-size-*, integer, [integer]); 573 } 574 575 @utility opacity-* { 576 opacity: calc(--value(integer) * 1%); 577 /* [!code highlight:2] */ 578 /* prettier-ignore */ 579 opacity: --value(--opacity-*, [percentage]); 580 } 581 ``` 582 583 #### Default values 584 585 Use `--default()` inside `--value()` to support a default value when the utility is used without an explicit value: 586 587 ```css 588 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 589 /* [!code word:--default(4)] */ 590 @utility tab-* { 591 tab-size: --value(integer, --default(4)); 592 } 593 ``` 594 595 This matches both `tab-2` and `tab-4`, as well as just `tab` which uses the default value of `4`: 596 597 ```css 598 /* [!code filename:Compiled CSS] */ 599 /* [!code highlight:4] */ 600 .tab { 601 tab-size: 4; 602 } 603 604 .tab-2 { 605 tab-size: 2; 606 } 607 ``` 608 609 The `--default()` function can also be used inside `--modifier()` to provide a default value when no modifier is present: 610 611 ```css 612 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 613 /* [!code word:--default(1)] */ 614 @utility tab-* { 615 tab-size: --value(integer); 616 line-height: --modifier(integer, --default(1)); 617 } 618 ``` 619 620 This matches `tab-2/3` with a line-height of `3`, and `tab-2` with a line-height of `1`. 621 622 #### Negative values 623 624 To support negative values, register separate positive and negative utilities into separate declarations: 625 626 ```css 627 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 628 @utility inset-* { 629 inset: --spacing(--value(integer)); 630 inset: --value([percentage], [length]); 631 } 632 633 /* [!code highlight:4] */ 634 @utility -inset-* { 635 inset: --spacing(--value(integer) * -1); 636 inset: calc(--value([percentage], [length]) * -1); 637 } 638 ``` 639 640 #### Modifiers 641 642 Modifiers are handled using the `--modifier()` function which works exactly like the `--value()` function but operates on a modifier if present: 643 644 ```css 645 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 646 @utility text-* { 647 /* prettier-ignore */ 648 font-size: --value(--text-*, [length]); 649 /* [!code highlight:2] */ 650 /* prettier-ignore */ 651 line-height: --modifier(--leading-*, [length], [*]); 652 } 653 ``` 654 655 If a modifier isn't present, any declaration depending on a modifier is just not included in the output. 656 657 #### Fractions 658 659 To handle fractions, we rely on the CSS `ratio` data type. If this is used with `--value()`, it's a signal to Tailwind to treat the value and modifier as a single value: 660 661 ```css 662 /* [!code filename:CSS] */ 663 @utility aspect-* { 664 /* [!code word:ratio, \[ratio\]] */ 665 /* prettier-ignore */ 666 aspect-ratio: --value(--aspect-ratio-*, ratio, [ratio]); 667 } 668 ``` 669 670 This will match utilities like `aspect-square`, `aspect-3/4`, and `aspect-[7/9]`. 671 672 ## Adding custom variants 673 674 In addition to using the variants that ship with Tailwind, you can also add your own custom variants using the `@custom-variant` directive: 675 676 ```css 677 @custom-variant theme-midnight { 678 &:where([data-theme="midnight"] *) { 679 @slot; 680 } 681 } 682 ``` 683 684 Now you can use the `theme-midnight:` variant in your HTML: 685 686 ```html 687 688 689 690 691 ``` 692 693 You can create variants using the shorthand syntax when nesting isn't required: 694 695 ```css 696 @custom-variant theme-midnight (&:where([data-theme="midnight"] *)); 697 ``` 698 699 When a custom variant has multiple rules, they can be nested within each other: 700 701 ```css 702 @custom-variant any-hover { 703 @media (any-hover: hover) { 704 &:hover { 705 @slot; 706 } 707 } 708 } 709 ``` 710
